<description>
The C++ Core Guidelines recommend **establishing an error handling strategy early in a project's design** ([E.1](https://isocpp.github.io/CppCoreGuidelines/CppCoreGuidelines#re-design)). Under the presumption that "we are still early" and given the fact that there is lots of development (eg #34931, #35003, #34132, ...) without such a strategy, it might be the right time to come up with a design document.

I post this as a PR rather than an Issue, because it will simplify giving feedback on individual parts of the text.
</description>

[2026-10-09] c:6078645811 comment by purpleKarrot (member):
[quoted text omitted]

Yes, that's what I'm getting at.

I have strong opinions about nullable arguments, which I see as related to the infamous "Boolean Trap", and about [passing pointers as function arguments](https://sched.co/2RT6N) in general. But those are separate from the question of error handling.

The question here is really: "Should functions be required to terminate on precondition violations?" I feel less strongly about whether they actually terminate, as long as the violation isn't presented as a runtime failure or used to produce an otherwise invalid result. Doing nothing may be perfectly valid behavior for a function. But if that's how it handles this input, then that input is already part of the domain it supports.

[quoted text omitted]
Yes. According to Hyrum's Law, the function already has a wider contract in practice. Updating the documentation would bring it into line with that behavior. Documenting a restriction just to reserve the right to enforce it later is unlikely to work well: callers may already depend on the behavior, regardless of what the documentation says.

And yes to the assertion question as well. That's what an assertion expresses: a condition that must hold for the code to proceed correctly. The same reasoning applies to preconditions: they state what must hold for the function to fulfill its contract. If the function can correctly handle the condition being false, then that condition isn't actually required and shouldn't be presented as such.

[quoted text omitted]
I didn't mean to imply that you were. Sorry, I should have been clearer about whom I was responding to. That was a separate point addressing “this isn't how we've been doing things” and “doesn't reflect existing practice” elsewhere in the discussion.

I think we're getting closer on the first point. Your example describes a function that can safely handle an input its documentation excludes. The documentation should reflect that behavior. My concern is with continuing when the assumptions needed for correctness no longer hold. Precondition violations should also not be treated as runtime failures or affect the function's return value. I'm well aware that the standard library doesn't always follow this guideline, but I still think it's the right goal for the code we control.
